analysis.one_liner: Makes the IRS's free online tax filing program permanent law and bars deals limiting it.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would make the IRS's free Direct File program permanent law, was introduced March 4, 2026 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, with 126 House Democrats cosponsoring.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill writes the IRS's free Direct File program — where taxpayers file federal returns online at no cost using data the government already has — into law, so it cannot be discontinued by a future administration or a future agreement. It also bans any deal between the IRS and tax-preparation companies that restricts the government from offering its own filing services, and voids existing such agreements. It sets requirements for the program: pre-filled data from IRS records, plain language, multiple languages, mobile access, live chat help, and promotion so people know it exists, and it pushes employers and banks to send tax documents earlier so returns can be pre-filled accurately.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers who currently pay commercial tax-preparation companies or spend hours on complicated software would be able to file federal returns free, online, with their data pre-filled from IRS records. The bill particularly helps lower- and middle-income filers who use paid software but have simple returns, and it requires the tool to be accessible in multiple languages, on mobile devices, and with live help. States that integrate their income taxes would get $1 million grants to make state filing seamless too.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers who currently pay to file

how_it_helps.text: Creates a permanent, federally owned online program where taxpayers can prepare and file federal returns at no charge, using IRS data to pre-fill information.

Bars the Treasury Secretary from entering into (or continuing) any agreement restricting the government from providing tax preparation or filing services, voiding existing such agreements within 30 days.
Requires the program to be available in multiple languages, on mobile devices, and with live chat support, and to be promoted through a mass marketing campaign so eligible taxpayers know it exists.

Requires the program to cover at least half of taxpayers in participating states starting after 2027, with continued expansion, and lets states integrate their own income tax filing for a $1 million grant.
Moves information-return deadlines earlier (generally March 31 for electronic returns) so the IRS has employers' and banks' data before taxpayers file, enabling more accurate pre-filled returns.

analysis.who_pays: Commercial tax-preparation and software companies would lose customers and revenue, since taxpayers could switch to the free government option; the bill also voids the IRS-industry agreement that has restricted government filing services. Employers and financial institutions would face earlier deadlines for sending wage and income data to the IRS. The program's operating costs would fall on federal appropriations.

drawbacks.text: The program only reaches taxpayers in 'participating States' — states that either integrate their income tax with the federal tool or have no state income tax — so residents of states that opt out would remain dependent on paid software.

The free federal tool would compete with commercial tax software and preparers, and the bill voids the existing IRS agreement that currently restrains the government from offering preparation services, drawing a direct challenge to that industry's business model.

The bill authorizes appropriations 'such sums as may be necessary' through 2035, so the program's cost to taxpayers falls on general federal funding, and it shifts filing responsibility and accuracy to taxpayers without charging fees.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is free, government-run tax filing with pre-filled data, saving households roughly hundreds of dollars in preparation fees or hours of paperwork; the costs are IRS implementation funding and the loss of the IRS-industry non-compete agreement that tax-prep companies rely on, which is precisely the point of the bill. The design is credible: it requires plain-language, multilingual, mobile-accessible software with live help, and mandates expansion to at least half of taxpayers in participating states while barring fees.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on March 4, 2026 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, where it has sat with no action since.

narrative.text: The bill's only actions to date are introduction and referral to the Ways and Means Committee on March 4, 2026.
126 of 217 House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans are listed as cosponsors.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, the tax-preparation industry is better off: the free federal filing alternative remains uncodified while the bill sits in committee.

for.name: Brad Sherman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to codify the Direct File program and void IRS agreements restricting government tax filing services.

against.name: Tax-preparation industry (Intuit, H&R Block and allied groups)
against.role: Commercial tax software and preparation companies
against.what_they_did: Has a long, widely reported history of lobbying against government-run free filing programs like Direct File and of funding the IRS agreement such agreements restrict.

sides.party_line_note: All 126 cosponsors are House Democrats; no Republicans are listed as sponsors or cosponsors.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software industry
industries.note: A free, government-run filing tool with pre-filled IRS data competes directly with paid software and preparers, and the bill voids the existing agreement that has blocked the government from offering such a service. Consumers who now pay for filing could switch to the free option.

industries.industry: Payroll and financial institutions filing information returns
industries.note: The bill moves W-2, 1099 and similar reporting deadlines earlier (generally March 31 for electronic filings), requiring employers and banks to furnish data sooner each year.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Ways and Means Committee with no markup or floor action scheduled and no Republican cosponsors, in a chamber controlled by Republicans. Bills in this position rarely reach the House floor, and even if it passed the House it would face a Republican-controlled Senate. Its most likely path is to die quietly at the end of the Congress, unless the Direct File program's fate becomes a larger public issue.
